raw_case_text:
In time, the patient, now 6 years old, developed obesity with normal stature and head circumference (see Figure 1), and no other manifestation. A younger brother, born in 2017, is also asymptomatic, in apparent good health (Figure 2).
Two teenage girl twins from Western Mexico were referred to INER for recurrent respiratory infections. They had a history of microcephaly and facial dysmorphism, with growth and psychomotor delay. Born pre-term (at 32 weeks of gestation) to non-consanguineous parents, the patients had three healthy elder siblings, and a pet dog.
During their first months of life, they suffered from 3 to 4 pneumoniae, gastroenteritis, and urinary tract infections. By 13 years of life, when they were referred to the National Institute of Pediatrics, they had developed moderate generalized jaundice with hepatosplenomegaly.
On physical examination, short stature (below percentile 10), low weight, mild to moderate mental retardation and speech delay were noted, with microcephaly below p3, a prominent mid-face with long nose, and micrognathia with a protruding tongue (see Figure 1). They had primary amenorrhea with absent secondary sexual features. A chest CT documented diffuse bilateral bronchiectasis; abdominal ultrasound and a barium swallow revealed portal hypertension with esophageal varices.
Laboratory workup showed persistent mild leukopenia with lymphopenia. Since around age twelve, they developed progressive pancytopenia: Hb 8g/dL, lymphocytes 210-300/mm3, less than 500 neutrophils, and 120,000 platelets; as well as elevated liver enzymes: increased conjugated bilirubin, ALT, AST, GGT, alkaline phosphatase, high ferritin (over 600 ng/ml), low fibrinogen (100 mg/dL), and high triglycerides (300 mg/dl). All serum immunoglobulins and lymphocyte subsets (CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, CD19+, CD16/56+) were also low: IgG 105-169 mg/dL, IgM 8.96-26.6 mg/dL, IgA < 6.67 mg/dL, IgE 1.1-1.5 IU/mL. A bone marrow aspirate reported medullary aplasia. Cellular radiosensitivity (radiomimetic assay) was negative to bleomycin; serologic tests for HepA, HepB, HepC, CMV, and EBV came back negative. Liver biopsy reported portal fibrosis with perivascular cell infiltration, suggestive of obstructive cirrhosis.
A provisional diagnosis of Nijmegen breakage syndrome (NBS) with bone marrow failure and sclerosing cholangitis was given. They continued treatment with prophylactic antibiotics and monthly intravenous gammaglobulin (IVIG), as well as ursodeoxycholic acid, molgramostin (GM-CSF), and oral transfer factor (leukocyte dialysate). They died 2 years apart at ages 14 and 16, at their hometown hospital, one twin of sudden massive gastrointestinal bleeding, and the other of sepsis and multiorgan failure (with pneumonia, anuria, and a distended abdomen). No autopsy was performed.
NBN was amplified and sequenced in Berlin with no mutations found. Years later, a targeted exome panel (Illumina TruSight) performed at INMEGEN in Mexico, revealed a compound heterozygous mutation in LIG4, consisting of the same 5 base-pair deletion as that of family A (c.1271_1275delAAAGA) in allele 1 (p. K424RfsX20), and a missense point mutation (c.745A>G) in allele 2 (p.M249V); both previously reported in patients with LIG4 deficiency (transcript NM_206937.1; LIG4base, www.ensembl.org), and predicted to be deleterious/probably damaging by both SIFT and PolyPhen. The p.M249V variant is absent from population databases such as gnomAD exomes; it is also predicted to be deleterious/probably damaging by all: DANN, GERP, dbNSFP, FATHMM, LRT, MetaLR, MetaSVM, MutationAssessor, MutationTaster, and PROVEAN in silico predictors.

subjective.chief_complaint: Teenage female twins from Western Mexico presented at age 13 with a lifelong history of recurrent sinopulmonary, gastrointestinal, and urinary tract infections, severe microcephaly, growth and psychomotor delay, progressive pancytopenia, and jaundice with hepatosplenomegaly.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born preterm at 32 weeks' gestation to non-consanguineous parents, both twin sisters experienced 3-4 episodes of pneumonia, gastroenteritis, and urinary tract infections in early infancy, progressive pancytopenia beginning around age 12, and moderate generalized jaundice, hepatosplenomegaly, portal hypertension, and bilateral bronchiectasis by age 13.
subjective.past_medical_history: Preterm birth at 32 weeks' gestation; congenital microcephaly, facial dysmorphism, growth failure, mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, speech delay, and primary amenorrhea. Family/social history: non-consanguineous parents, three healthy older siblings, pet dog.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for recurrent respiratory, GI, and urinary infections, jaundice, abdominal distension, primary amenorrhea, and terminal massive GI bleeding (one twin at age 14) and pneumonia/anuria/sepsis (second twin at age 16).

objective.physical_examination: Short stature (<10th percentile), low weight, microcephaly (<3rd percentile), bird-like facial dysmorphism (prominent mid-face, long nose, micrognathia, protruding tongue), mild-to-moderate intellectual disability and speech delay, absent secondary sexual characteristics, moderate generalized jaundice, and hepatosplenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Progressive pancytopenia from age 12: hemoglobin 8 g/dL, absolute lymphocytes 210-300/mm3, ANC <500/mm3, and platelets 120,000/mm3. Elevated conjugated bilirubin, ALT, AST, GGT, and ALP; elevated ferritin (>600 ng/mL), low fibrinogen (100 mg/dL), and hypertriglyceridemia (300 mg/dL). Pan-hypogammaglobulinemia: IgG 105-169 mg/dL, IgM 8.96-26.6 mg/dL, IgA <6.67 mg/dL, and IgE 1.1-1.5 IU/mL. Viral serologies for HAV, HBV, HCV, cytomegalovirus (CMV), and EBV were negative; cellular bleomycin radiomimetic sensitivity assay was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and barium swallow demonstrated portal hypertension and esophageal varices.
objective.advanced_workup: Flow cytometry showed depletion across all lymphocyte subsets (CD3+, CD4+, CD8+, CD19+, CD16/56+). Chest CT demonstrated diffuse bilateral bronchiectasis. Bone marrow aspirate showed medullary aplasia; percutaneous liver biopsy showed portal fibrosis with perivascular cellular infiltration suggestive of obstructive cirrhosis/sclerosing cholangitis. While NBN sequencing was negative, targeted next-generation exome sequencing (Illumina TruSight) identified compound heterozygous pathogenic mutations in LIG4: a 5-bp frameshift deletion in allele 1 (c.1271_1275delAAAGA, p.K424RfsX20) and a missense mutation in allele 2 (c.745A>G, p.M249V).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive genetic diagnosis of DNA ligase IV (LIG4) deficiency syndrome (confirmed postmortem by compound heterozygous LIG4 mutations c.1271_1275delAAAGA [p.K424RfsX20] and c.745A>G [p.M249V] after ruling out Nijmegen breakage syndrome [NBN] and viral hepatitis/CMV/EBV) presenting with microcephaly, primordial dwarfism, combined immunodeficiency, bone marrow aplasia, bronchiectasis, and sclerosing cholangitis/portal hypertension. Managed palliatively with prophylactic antibiotics, monthly IVIG, ursodeoxycholic acid, GM-CSF (molgramostin), and oral leukocyte dialysate transfer factor; the twins died at ages 14 and 16 of massive variceal/gastrointestinal hemorrhage and septic multiorgan failure, respectively.
